		Sara Bareilles on ‘Good Grief’ and Finding Joy in the Tough Stuff: ‘Grief Is the Mothership of This Record, but It Carries Release, Hope, Optimism and Connection’
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Getty Images for IMDb
	

		
	
				

	She could have called it “Great Grief,” but that would have been immodest. Sara Bareilles‘ “Good Grief,” her first new studio album in seven years, is one of the year’s finest achievements from a singer-songwriter… and its purely musical delights are such that you might feel that way about it even if you haven’t been through some shit, as they say. 

	If you have, all the better to relate to the record and its sometimes somber, sometimes playful meditations on a whole catalog of grief (and grievances): losing best friends to death at too early an age, dealing with fertility struggles, running to and away from the precipice of love, eroding women’s rights, mental health issues, and the challenges of continuing to believe in the promise of America. 

	Variety had an in-depth conversation with Bareilles about the new album and many of the tough or inspiring issues related to it — along with touching on a recently released documentary film that captures some of the making of the record, “Sara Bareilles: Good Grief,” and her first real tour of the 2020s, which has just gotten underway and includes dates Sept. 18-19 at Radio City Music Hall and Oct. 12-14 at L.A.’s Dolby Theatre. (Scroll down to see a full list of tour dates.)

	You’ve gone a pretty long time between solo albums now. Of course you’ve had “Girls5Eva” and composing your next stage musical (“The Interestings”) and plenty of other things occupying yout time.  Does it feel any different putting this one out into the world now than in times past?

	It does feel different. It’s been a minute since I’ve done this. … But I feel pretty peaceful with the “it takes the time it takes” kind of method around this part of my life. I tend towards a pretty hefty amount of time between records anyway. It takes me a long time to have something else to say. It’s been seven years since my last record, and hopefully it was somewhat worth the wait. I was writing about this this morning; I journal every morning. I found so much catharsis and healing in the making of this record, just going through this period of time with the loss of friends and just the hardships that have happened over the last handful of years in my own personal journey. I felt so grateful to get to put some of those experiences somewhere. So it feels like the timing is right on time, for me personally. I’m hoping it lands for the audience in that way as well.

	There are “mature themes” on this record. A lot of your audience has sort of grown up with you and dealt with at least some of these same things you’re writing about. Do you suppose you have to have a certain amount of life experience to relate to an album like this? Or if someone is 20 and hasn’t really lost anybody yet in this life, can they still be impacted by it the same way?

	It’s like, yeah, did I make an old person’s record? [Laughs.] In some ways, yeah, I think what I was attuned to when I was much younger, in my late teens and 20s, the stuff that really kept me up at night, it usually had to do with matters of the heart, like a fixation on a romantic love. But I do feel like, as like a global community, the world feels like it has, I would say, wisened. I think I mean we’ve all sort of aged up a little bit together. I feel this in my young nieces and my younger sister and friends that I have that are much younger: There is a kind of awareness about things that I was not as attuned to. I don’t know if it’s about the existential drama of life and death, but I do think that there is a kind of antenna turned towards bigger-picture themes than maybe I was quite aware of when I was that age. I see these young people dealing with the climate crisis and watching what’s happened politically and how divided our world feels. And the way they feel amid the emotionality of the drama of your youth — I do feel like there’s a lot of grief in there. And I don’t think anybody ever called it that for me. But I’m really curious to hear feedback about who relates to this and who doesn’t.

	This album is kind of bookended with songs at the beginning and end that deal with grief in a more obvious way, maybe, with death and loss. But you touch on a lot of subjects. Is there a way in which you thought of “Good Grief” as kind of a concept album where even the songs that aren’t so overtly about that are also themed to grief?

	There’s a line in the sons called “Ladies in a Line,” and the lyric is “Grief is the blanket, and it covers everything.” I do think that grief is sort of like the mothership of this record. It’s like the home base for all of these experiences… I think that what I’ve learned about grief in my own personal relationship to the experience of it is that it’s not just one thing. It carries joy, it carries release, it carries hope and optimism and connection and a lot of really buoyant themes. So yeah, I think that even a song like “Idiot Heart,” which is about wanting to be led to the edge by a kind of an urgency towards love, there is grief in that too, because what we love, we lose. And so I can kind of find it in everything. But I don’t look at it as a somber experience. I just look at it as a really rich experience.


	I was recommending the album to a young woman who had lost her mother not that long ago and still has some trauma over that, and when I described it as an album largely inspired by grief, she was like, “Is this gonna destroy me?” And I answered, “No, I don’t think it is, actually.” It’s like, the song about losing your best friend, “Just a Kid,” is so joyful, in its way. That’s followed by “Still Crying,” which is sort of a happy-sounding song, even though it’s about not being able to stop weeping. So the album has this upbeat spirit and does not get bogged down in sorrow, even though it’s kind of unflinching at the same time.

	I thought so. Well, thanks for sharing that. I’m really sorry for the loss. Talk about a transformative moment to be going through… I don’t know. I think I was always really afraid of the big feelings, especially when I was younger, just afraid that I wouldn’t be able to hold the bigness of feeling. And it’s been interesting — I think a lot of people relate to that. We’re sort of afraid of sadness and afraid of grief, and it’s so understandable, but there’s a lot of wisdom… a lot to get out of it, too.



	The songs that deal overtly with grief on this are not all about the same person, or even all from your personal point of view. You have separate songs for two of your best friends, Chad and Gavin. But the opening number, “Home,” was inspired by a podcast conversation between Stephen Colbert and Anderson Cooper. Which I completely did not realize the first time I listened to the album and wrote something public about it. I did realize that a person in the song talked about being 54 and having a son, but I was still slow in picking up the clues this was not about you…

	Sorry!

	Not your fault! It should have been clear enough at a point. Anyway, articles like this help fill in the backstory for other people. So, in being inspired by this conversation between Colbert and Cooper, would you say you were recreating what they said in your own words for the song?

	That’s exactly right. I listened to their incredible conversation on Anderson’s podcast called “All There Is,” and it’s just a beautiful, tender offering. It was very moving to me to hear two men discuss grief in great detail, and how the echoes of loss lived inside their physical homes as children and then as adults. I was really struck by, I think it’s Stephen in the conversation — I have to go back and refresh my memory — but one of them starts talking about just how important it is to tell the story. How important re the stories about our own lives, about what we lose, about just who we are — that’s what we have to gift each other. It became sort of a thematic cornerstone to the record, and the song “Home” is kind of the invitation. It’s the first song for a reason: it’s the invitation into this exchange of stories.



	Have you had a chance to talk to either Cooper or Colbert, to tell them that they’re in this song?

	Yeah, I’ve shared it with both of them. I got a chance to go on Anderson’s podcast, actually, and I played it for him live on the podcast. He had a beautiful, very emotional reaction to it. And Stephen, I sent it to him via email, and we had a sweet exchange. They both remarked how uncanny it is that a conversation can transmute and become something totally different … that a conversation they had on a podcast would turn into a piece of music. I love that. I love that about music in general, that the seeds for these songs and these ideas come from all kinds of places.



	For me, maybe the most powerful number is the second track, “Just a Kid.” It’s a great example of how the personal can be universal, since nearly every line in it is something specific related to your late friend, and we can’t co-sign all of those exact experiences you had of him. Yet it’s all the better for being something so grounded in reality. The lyrics have kind of a fun writing trick where you have quick and sometimes contrary lines, like “My first best friend / I’ll never see again / You never got to get married/ And I hate where you’re buried.” It’s got some mirth as well as being sad, and if you were writing your next musical, it feels like it could be the 11 o’clock number.

	Oh, that’s awesome. It was such a love letter to my friend Chad, and there’s a lot of nostalgia in this song, conceptually, in wanting to honor the period of time where we really were attached at the hip. This was like early aughts, and going on tour for the first time, and we were roommates, and we did literally everything together. It’s like a sense memory, a felt kind of timeline. We were listening to a lot of Frou Frou and Counting Crows and the Wallflowers. Like, the soundtrack to our lives was very particular. And so I wanted to dip into the feeling of that time and make it feel like a celebration of his life, which it really ended up being. It’s a heartbreaking lyric for me to sing, because it was born of loss, but it’s so joyful because it just brings his whole essence to mind, and I love getting to sing about him from the mountaintop, so to speak. I love getting to share his legacy in song.



	There’s a slightly meta aspect to “Just a Kid” in that you have the chorus, where you’re describing the experience of singing into your phone as you are writing the song on a city street, and not caring what onlookers think. It sounds like you were unafraid to be in front of strangers having this kind of personal musical experience.

	Yeah, totally. I was on my way home from the grocery store, and my hands were full, and I just could feel the arrival of this song. But it was more of just a sense of Chad. I felt that there was something like a transmission happening. And I put my grocery bags down and started singing into my phone on the street.

	It also brings to mind a couple of times I’ve talked to friends about things like this. And I had an experience with my grandfather where I was singing. I knew he was going to pass, and I was across the country and wouldn’t be able to get there in time, so I was singing “Amazing Grace” into the phone. I just think of all those times, so many people, who we can’t physically be with each other. If you happen to know someone’s at the end, how many people are singing or saying something into a phone and just counting on those telephone wires to carry the love? I guess they’re not telephone wires anymore; they’re digital pixels in the air. But just that idea of crossing a great amount of distance. And I think about that between the living and the dead, but also between the living and the living, too.



	Just to take a little bit of a thematic turn: “Hands Off My Body” makes its studio-recording premiere on this album after you debuted it at the Hollywood Bowl a couple of summers ago. Andthat gets into a different kind of grief/anger. Was there was a particular prompt that inspired either that or the other sort of faintly political song, “Heartland,” which seems to be sung from the point of view of the Statue of Liberty.

	Yeah. Oh my God, a litany of reasons. “Hands Off My Body,” the seeds of that particular song were actually born after the Iranian women’s movement, after Mahsa Amini’s death and the Women, Life, Freedom movement that I found to be just an extraordinary showing of strength and resilience. And then, in terms of timeline, I had written that song back then, but then Roe v. Wade fell, and abortion rights started getting repealed all over, and women’s health initiatives were stripped away, and the Epstein files come out. It was just one thing after another, after another. I think there is a side of grief that is rageful, and that’s a lot of rage around the oppressive and consistent lack of respect and autonomy for women and their bodies. So I think I’m glad I had a place to put some of that. I still feel rageful about that.



	And to speak about “Heartland,” I think as we’ve watched this second Trump administration unfold with such recklessness and cruelty, frankly, I just started thinking about how sad I am that the idea of patriotism has been co-opted. I do still love this country, flaws and deeply problematic history and all, and I grieve that there isn’t more space for that sometimes I believe in the ideals that we’re building towards. So writing a song from the perspective of the Statue of Liberty or from the perspective of the Constitution and these ideas and words on a page that I think are still worth fighting for — it’s complicated. It’s not one thing or another, but I do believe that fighting for the ideas that this country is built on is still a worthy pursuit.



	Try to tell a younger person that you are considering putting a flag in the flagpole for a major holiday and that is an invitation to get an incredulous look.

	Yeah. I think it’s important to remember that we have to be able to hold both in our minds, that we have to love something that is complicated. And I’m not diminishing the depth to which there are really problematic parts of the way our systems run and the way the country was formed and founded. But I don’t want to throw it all away. So I grieve the feeling that you have to sometimes.



	With “Ladies in a Line,” which is a song about feelings coming up at a fertility clinic, I was thinking about how great it would sound in the middle of a musical…

	Yeah. I didn’t get that far in my mind about it.

	But do you think that writing for the theater has changed the way you write for a singer-songwriter record?

	Oh, I’m for sure thinking that it has. It has absolutely made a massive impact on my writing. I just am not thinking, “Am I making a musical out of this material or not?” But no, I feel it deeply. Even just from a form perspective, a lot of these songs don’t follow a more traditional pop song format, which I tended to stick more closely to in my past writing. Lots of these songs are a little more formless, and they’re telling a story. There’s less repetition and less in the way of, like, classic choruses. So that just feels like an evolution of my writing that has definitely been influenced by the theater.

	But with that song, I really wanted to name the experience of fertility and what is hard about it and what is universal about it. Well, I don’t know about entirely universal, but it is certainly a very deeply shared experience with millions and millions and millions of women and families trying to conceive all over the world. It just struck me during my own continued journey with fertility that there’s a lot of people here, and I just didn’t have a sense of how many, many, many, many people need support. So even though you’re having this really quite typical, un-unique experience, it can feel very lonely. So my hope was just to — I don’t know — name it. Just name it for the sake of naming it.





	In another song, “Capsize Me,” you have a line that perhaps describes how you think of yourself in relation to your audience sometimes: “And the part of me who shudders can be a lighthouse for the others who need to find the shore when they are lost at sea.” That seems to sort of accept responsibility, or at least awareness, that you can be a stand-in or an avatar for a lot of people who are going through heavy experiences and that you’re grateful accept that as part of what you do, whether it’s the initial impulse or not.

	Hmm. Yeah. I appreciate you saying that. I take a lot of really deep pride in that piece of it. I don’t know if it’s pride; it’s comfort. I do feel a kind of responsibility to speak really honestly about the places in my life that carry hardship, and the places where I feel fear, and vulnerability, and anxiety, and all of those things. And if my struggles can bring comfort to someone else, I’m so happy to have them. Well, “happy to have them” is maybe an overstatement. But I am willing to have them because I think that it’s a real privilege to get to try to translate some of these experiences into something that might bring a little bit of comfort. That’s my great hope for this record, is that it just brings a little bit of comfort.




	In the past, occasionally, you’ve been on social media being public about mental health struggles. Fans might think that there’s such wisdom in your songwriting, and you’re married, and of course you seem like the consummate pro as a musician, to the point of imagiing that you are too together and have too much going for you to have those same issues with it they do. But of course you can be wise and you can be a pro and those things are still not always buffers against being a mess.
	

	Yeah. I feel like the thing I keep learning over and over again is that there is no “you figured it out” plateau. When I was younger, I really, in all my naiveté, thought there was a kind of happiness plateau, that you figure out how to be happy in this life. And it’s been a really mind-opening experience to understand, and then understand yet again and yet again, that there is no plateau, that we’re just on this very dynamic, often volatile, often uncomfortable roller coaster ride of being alive. And sometimes we’re hanging on for dear life, and sometimes we’re thrillseekers with our arms up, enjoying the descent, you know? I really am trying to just embrace all of it, to stay really open and willing to receive what’s kinda coming at me, and coming at all of us.

	There are so many things that can be a carrot on a stick — finding love, employment, financial security… and fixing yourself can be a carrot on a stick, too.

	Yes. Truly, truly. Nothing to fix.
	

	A question that has less to do with the emotional content of the album and just how you completed it: When we spoke when your documentary was premiering at a film festival some months back, you said that people should be aware that the initial recording sessions that were captured in the doc did not represent the entire recording at all, and the finished product would not necessarily sound like what is in that film, but that it captured a important moment in time. Then, of course, you went on and worked with Aaron Dessner, and did a lot of overdubbing on the raw tracks we see in the movie as well as additional songs. So you felt comfortable having a snapshot of the album in progress, as something that you spent a lot more time on.

	Yeah. Even with that idea, though, we’re always changing, too. Like, if I finished the record this month, I would probably make a million different decisions. It is the thing that I love about making records, though. It’s like it really is, as you said, just a snapshot. It’s a snapshot of a set of circumstances and the way you are feeling in a moment, and you do the best you can to make something that you think you can live with for a while. But inevitably, you change, and your feelings about the song itself changes. I mean, I’m even noticing that as we prepare to go on tour, where there’s just little things that live differently in the space and time of putting it on stage live. So it will be, yet again, another snapshot of a song that will hopefully go through a lot of evolution in its lifespan.

	So, yeah, I feel really good at this stage in my life, and for where I am kind of spiritually and emotionally, about transparency, and just letting people can see where things began. And I appreciate the opportunity to have people trust that I’m gonna try to take you somewhere where I want the song to live. And if anyone’s seen me in concert, they know I keep fucking with these songs till the end of time, so they’re very different now on stage than they were when they were recorded. But that’s part of the fun.

	Are you enjoying having that proximity of the album and the film coming out pretty close together, so that a lot of your fans are experiencing the two things pretty close to simultaneously?
	

	I’m loving it. It feels like a giant art project, the whole thing —  the album, the tour, the film and this installation we’re doing at Lincoln Center to celebrate the album release. I think we’re taking really good care of the music, which is the thing that matters the most to me. So I think delivering the process of creation and especially getting to tell the backstory a little bit as to where these songs actually came from, to me, it’s really honoring what this whole record is about. Which is, you know, about trying to metabolize and make sense of great loss and great pain, and hopefully turn it into something beautiful.

	(To read our previous interview with Bareilles talking about the “Good Grief” documentary, click here. For a review of the “Good Grief” album, click here.)

	International Oscar Submissions: Nepal, Singapore, Israel, Romania, South Korea, Chile and More Join the List
body:
Sep 13, 2026 1:14pm PT	
	

	
	International Oscar Submissions: Nepal, Singapore, Israel, Romania, South Korea, Chile and More Join the List
	



			
			
	
						

									©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection
	
					


								
		
				

	The campaigns for the Oscar for international feature film are gaining momentum, with final submissions due by Oct. 1. The Oscars shortlists will be revealed on Dec. 15, with 15 international films selected to be voted on by Academy members in all branches who commit to watch all 15 films. Oscar nominations will be revealed on Jan. 21.

	This year’s entries include titles like Romania’s “Fjord,” which won the Palme d’Or at Cannes; Chile’s “The Meltdown,” which screened in Un Certain Regard; and Germany’s “Everytime,” which won Cannes’ Un Certain Regard prize. 

	France has not yet submitted a film, but faces several disparate choices. 

	Meanwhile, a new Academy rule allows any film that wins the top prize at one of the six biggest festivals — Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Sundance, Busan and Toronto — to be entered in the international feature race even without a national committee’s backing. 


			
			
	Elephants in the Fog (Nepal)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of UTN, Les Valseurs, DGS				
					
				

	Nepal’s International Feature Film Selection Committee has chosen Abinash Bikram Shah’s “Elephants in the Fog” as the country’s entry for the 99th Academy Awards.

	The film marks Shah’s feature directorial debut and follows a Kinnar community in a Nepalese village fighting to protect itself. It premiered in the Un Certain Regard section of the Cannes Film Festival in May, where it won the section’s Jury Prize, and also picked up nominations for the Caméra d’Or and the Queer Palm. The cast is led by Pushpa Thing Lama, Deepika Yadav, Jasmine Bishwokarma, Aliz Ghimire and Dura Sanjay Kumar Gupta.

	The Oscars selection comes as “Elephants in the Fog” continues to expand its footprint in international markets. Sales company Best Friend Forever has closed deals in several territories, including MetFilm Distribution in the U.K., Filmin in Spain, Vedette in Benelux, Trigon in Switzerland, Lev Cinema in Israel, Jayantii in Australia, EFAR Films in India, PT Falcon in Indonesia and the Film Development Council of the Philippines, alongside an inflight deal with Silk Route. Those additions build on earlier deals covering France, Germany and Austria, Brazil and Nepal itself. The film is produced by Underground Talkies Nepal, Les Valseurs and Die Gesellschaft DGS.

		
			
			
	We Are All Strangers (Singapore)
			
										
					Image Credit: Giraffe Pictures				
					
				

	“We Are All Strangers,” written and directed by Anthony Chen, has been selected as Singapore‘s entry in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards.

	Set in contemporary Singapore, the film centers on family relationships and unexpected life changes. It stars Chen’s frequent collaborators Yeo Yann Yann and Koh Jia Ler, with Andi Lim and Regene Lim rounding out the cast. Earlier this year, it became the first Singaporean film selected for the main competition at the Berlin Film Festival.

	“We Are All Strangers” completes Chen’s Growing Up trilogy, which began with “Ilo Ilo” in 2013 and continued with “Wet Season” in 2019. The two earlier films have collectively won more than 50 international accolades, including five Golden Horse Awards, along with “Ilo Ilo‘s” Caméra d’Or win at Cannes. Both films previously served as Singapore’s Oscars entries, at the 86th and 93rd Academy Awards respectively.

		
			
			
	Tell Me Everything (Israel)
			
										
					Image Credit: Ziv Berkovich				
					
				

	Moshe Rosenthal’s “Tell Me Everything” has been voted Best Picture at Israel’s Ophir Awards, automatically making it the country’s submission for best international feature film category at the 99th Academy Awards.

	“Tell Me Everything,” set in the 1980s against the rising HIV epidemic, premiered at Sundance in the world cinema dramatic competition. It is Moshe Rosenthal’s sophomore feature. “Karaoke,” his directorial feature debut, premiered at the 2022 Tribeca Film Festival.

	“Tell Me Everything” follows Boaz (played by Yair Mazor), a 12-year-old who discovers a devastating secret about his father. Catching up with Boaz as an adult (played by “The Vanishing Soldier’s” Ido Tako), the film delves into their father-son relationship as they attempt to heal wounds and repair bonds. Assi Cohen (“Yossi & Jagger”) stars as Boaz’s father.

		
			
			
	Fjord (Romania)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Tudor Panduru				
					
				

	“Fjord,” written and directed by Cristian Mungiu, is Romania’s submission for the 2027 Oscars in the best international feature film category, having been unanimously chosen by the country’s selection committee.

	The film premiered in the official competition at the Cannes Film Festival, where it won the Palme d’Or for best film, the FIPRESCI Prize, the Ecumenical Jury Prize, the Prix de la Citoyenneté and the François Chalais Prize.

	Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve star in the lead roles, with cinematography by Tudor Vladimir Panduru, editing by Mircea Olteanu, and production design by Simona Pădurețu.

		
			
			
	Aontas (Ireland)
			
										
					Image Credit: Púca Pictures				
					
				

	“Aontas,” the Irish-language heist thriller from director Damian McCann, has been chosen as Ireland’s entry for the best international feature film category at the 2027 Academy Awards.

	The film was selected by the Irish Film & TV Academy (IFTA) and a committee including “Evil Dead Rise” director Lee Cronin, “Derry Girls” creator Lisa McGee, BAFTA-nominated director Brian Kirk (“Game of Thrones), BAFTA nominated director Kathryn Ferguson (“Nothing Compares”), Emmy-winning actress and filmmaker Aisha Tyler (“Friends”), actress Fionnuala Flaherty (“Kneecap”) and IFTA chief executive Áine Moriarty.

	Told in reverse chronology, “Aontas” follows three unlikely thieves, led by a woman on the verge of a breakdown, who rob a rural Irish bank. Opening in the tragic aftermath of the heist-gone-wrong. What starts as a poorly executed robbery becomes a portrait of a wilful woman trapped in her own past. It stars Carrie Crowley (“The Quiet Girl “), Bríd Brennan, Eva-Jane Gaffney, Seán T. Ó Meallaigh, Marcus Lamb and Art Parkinson.

		
			
			
	The Meltdown (Chile)
			
										
					Image Credit: 'The Meltdown'  Courtesy of Mubi				
					
				

	Chile’s Film Academy has selected “The Meltdown” (“El deshielo”) by Manuela Martelli, her post-Pinochet mystery drama set in an Andes ski resort, to represent the country in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Academy Awards. Martelli’s follow-up to her acclaimed drama “Chile, 1976” had its world premiere at Cannes’ prominent strand Un Certain Regard this year.

	“The Meltdown” stars Maya O’Rourke – in her film debut – who plays a nine-year-old at her family’s ski resort who witnesses unsettling events that will test her loyalties. Other cast members are Paulina Urrutia, Mauricio Pešutić, Paula Zúñiga, Marcela Salinas and Lautaro Cantillana.

		
			
			
	All of a Sudden (Japan)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Neon, Cannes Film Festival				
					
				

	Hamaguchi Ryusuke‘s “All of a Sudden” has been selected as Japan’s entry in the international feature category at the 99th Academy Awards, the Motion Picture Producers Association of Japan (Eiren) has revealed.

	The selection marks the second time a Hamaguchi film has represented Japan in the category, five years after “Drive My Car” won the international feature Oscar and picked up nominations for best picture, director and adapted screenplay at the 94th Academy Awards.

	“All of a Sudden” is a France-Japan co-production made with backing from Germany and Belgium, shot largely in Paris. The film draws on “When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn: Twenty Letters Between a Philosopher With Terminal Cancer and a Medical Anthropologist,” a book of correspondence by Miyano Makiko and Isono Maho. It follows Marie-Lou Fontaine (Virginie Efira), who runs a nursing home outside Paris and pushes to adopt a more dignity-focused model of elderly care, and Morisaki Mari (Okamoto Tao), a Japanese theater director undergoing cancer treatment. Nagatsuka Kyōzō and Kurosaki Kōdai round out the cast.

		
			
			
	Everytime (Germany)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of The Barricades				
					
				

	Sandra Wollner’s “Everytime” has been selected as Germany’s entry for the Academy Award for best international feature film.

	The film’s synopsis reads as follows: The last photograph Jessie took shows the sun over Berlin. It hangs there as if nothing had happened. But Ella has lost her daughter. What remains is Jessie’s younger sister and a complicated relationship with the boy everyone blames. The unlikely trio ends up on a family holiday that never really existed. Under the shimmering sun of Tenerife, memory and the present become inseparably intertwined. The ghosts are everywhere.

	“Everytime” celebrated its world premiere at the 79th Cannes Film Festival in May. Wollner’s third feature film, for which she also wrote the screenplay, was selected for the Un Certain Regard sidebar where it won the Prix Un Certain Regard, the section’s top award. Cannes was followed by invitations to the Sydney Film Festival and the Karlovy Vary Film Festival, among others. At the Sarajevo Film Festival, “Everytime” was awarded the Heart of Sarajevo Grand Prize. Its North American premiere will follow in September at the Toronto Film Festival. Other festival appearances include the New York Film Festival.

		
			
			
	Becoming Human (Cambodia)
			
										
					Image Credit: Anti-Archive				
					
				

	The Cambodia Oscar Selection Committee (COSC) has selected “Becoming Human,” directed by Polen Ly, as the country’s official submission for the international feature film category at the 99th Academy Awards.

	The film follows Thida, the spirit guardian of an aging cinema slated for demolition, as she weighs the choice of rebirth against her existence as a ghost. Her bond with Hai, a living man she meets along the way, pushes her to confront both her spiritual fate and a country in the midst of sweeping social change.

	“Becoming Human” is Ly’s debut feature. He previously made the short film “Further and Further Away” in 2022 and the documentary “Until the Orchid Blooms,” which premiered at IDFA in 2024 and won the grand prize at the Taiwan International Documentary Festival in 2026. The cast is led by 15-year-old newcomer and dance student Savorn Serak alongside Piseth Chhun, who won the Venice Horizons award for best actor in 2021 for his role in Kavich Neang’s “White Building.”

		
			
			
	Possible Love (South Korea)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Netflix, Venice Film Festival				
					
				

	The Korean Film Council (KOFIC) has selected “Possible Love,” directed by Lee Chang-dong, as South Korea‘s official entry for the international feature film category at the 2027 Academy Awards.

	“Possible Love” marks Lee’s first feature in eight years, following “Burning,” “Poetry” and “Secret Sunshine.” The film centers on two married couples whose lives intersect after a funeral: Mi-ok and her laid-off husband Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), who live quietly with their young son Cheol, and Ye-ji, a filmmaker making a documentary about workers who lost their jobs, and her husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). When Mi-ok agrees to be filmed by Ye-ji, the two women grow close, while Mi-ok finds herself unsettled by an attraction to Sang-woo. As the two couples’ worlds overlap, cracks begin to surface in both marriages.

	In its evaluation, the committee cited the film’s polished craftsmanship and the clarity of its directorial vision, pointing to the tone and mise-en-scène that sustain a sense of pressure throughout the story. The drama was described as prompting reflection on gentle forms of violence, incomplete freedom and the nature of true happiness, alongside a labor movement sequence that the committee said captured layered social undercurrents.

		
			
			
	Like a Limbless Tree (Turkey)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Tekhne Film				
					
				

	“Like a Limbless Tree,” an intimate social drama directed by Tunç Davut, has been selected as Turkey‘s entry for the Academy Award for best international feature film.

	Davut, whose previous works include the 2015 drama “Entanglement and TV series “Serçe” and “Kinali Kuzular,” delves into the fragility of human existence against a backdrop of the theme of immigration in “Like a Limbless Tree.” The film is produced by Istanbul-based Tekhne Film and stars Ali Ipin, Fayyaz Duman and Selen Kurtaran.

	Davut’s drama – which won an award at the Bosphorus Film Festival and was selected for the Antalya Golden Orange Film Festival and the Ankara Film Festival – is about a retired engineer named Refik whose life changes forever after being diagnosed with a terminal disease just as his Syrian caregiver disappears while attempting to flee to Europe, leaving him in charge of her two children.

		
			
			
	How to Divorce During the War (Lithuania)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of New Europe Film Sales				
					
				

	Andrius Blaževičius’ “How to Divorce During the War” has been selected as Lithuania’s entry for the Academy Award for best international feature film.

	Blaževičius’ third feature won the directing award in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition at the Sundance Film Festival. The film was picked up for theatrical distribution in North America by Zeitgeist Films, in association with Kino Lorber, and will be released on Aug. 21.

	Set in Vilnius in 2022, it’s a story of a high-flying executive Marija, who chooses the worst possible moment for an honest conversation with her husband Vytas about divorcing – just one day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine goes into full scale. Now the couple must navigate the process of separation as it collides with a refugee and mid-life crisis.

title: Ella Langley’s ‘Dandelion’ Album Returns to No. 1 Spot on Billboard 200 for First Time in Four Months, So ‘Choosin’ Texas’ Won’t Get Lonely at the Top
description: Ella Langely’s fans are choosing her “Dandelion” album as a complete piece of work, and not just staying entirely trained on her long-running “Choos
body:
Ella Langely’s fans are choosing her “Dandelion” album as a complete piece of work, and not just staying entirely trained on her long-running “Choosin’ Texas” smash. “Dandelion” has returned to the No. 1 spot on the Billboard 200 album chart for a third non-consecutive week at the top. Its previous stay at No. 1 was contained to the first two weeks it was out, in late April , but the album has rarely been too far from the summit in the intervening four and a half months.
	

	With the re-ascent of “Dandelion” on the album chart, probably no one needs to be told that this means Langley is again topping both of Billboard’s primary charts, as the indomitable “Choosin’ Texas” remained at No. 1 on the most recent Hot 100 singles chart to be released. The next Hot 100 will be made public on Monday, and chances are good that “Texas” will still be on top, which would mark the song’s 22nd week at No. 1. If that turns out to be the case, Langley will have tied Mariah Carey’s all-time record of 22 weeks for “All I Want for Christmas is You” and be one week away from breaking the record.

	“Dandelion” benefited from the ongoing hunger for all things Langley, but also from a Labor Day holiday period in which there were no huge albums debuting. It reached the summit with 67,000 equivalent album units. That’s pretty much par for the recent course for Langley’s album; that figure was down just 1% from the previous week for her. But as Billboard pointed out, 67,000 was the lowest number for a No. 1 album in more than a year. (The last time an album was No. 1 with fewer units was in May 2025, when SZA’s “SOS” topped the chart with just 52,000.)
	

	The only new album to make the top 10 was Adela‘s first full-length alum, “Prima,” which bowed at No. 4 with 56,000. The numbers for Adela were tilted toward full-album sales, with 31,000; streaming (SEA) units were good for another 25,000 units, on the strength of 25.94 million on-demand streams. The album debuted at No. 1 on the album sales chart and No. 14 on the streaming albums chart.

	Beyoncé’s “B’Day” virtually counted as a new album, reentering the chart for the first time in 18 years due to a 20th anniversary deluxe reissue. It reentered at No. 8 with 38,000 units.

	Rounding out the top 10: Olivia Rodrigo, still riding high at No. 2 (with 64,000 units, down just 4%), followed by Morgan Wallen at No. 3, Noah Kahan at No. 5, Ariana Grande at No. 6 (up nine spots thanks to a deluxe edition with live tracks coming out), Rod Wave at No. 7 (down six spots and 57% after debuting at No. 1 a week ago), Drake at No. 9 and Olivia Dean at No. 10.

title: ‘On Behalf of My Son’ Review: A Strained Brazilian Drama About a Mother’s Apology Tour
description: A Brazilian drama with a powerful premise but labored execution, Gabriel Martins’ “On Behalf of My Son” follows the ripple effects of a tragic bus a
body:
A Brazilian drama with a powerful premise but labored execution, Gabriel Martins’ “On Behalf of My Son” follows the ripple effects of a tragic bus accident through the eyes of the driver’s mother, Vicentina (Rejane Faria). As she pillories herself with an apology tour, family members of the other victims veer in and out of the spotlight, offering more potentially affecting moments which — by structural necessity — quickly fade from view. Instead, the dramatic focus pivots entirely around Faria’s performance, which unfortunately works against the movie, more often than not.
	

	Opening with unassuming portraits of passengers on their commute in the city of Belo Horizonte, “On Behalf of My Son” begins with an enticing visual setup for individual stories that don’t fully materialize. In the moment, however, Martins imbues tremendous intrigue through snippets of the seemingly distracted middle-aged driver, Wesley (Renato Novaes), and eventually, through the crash itself. Its presentation is shocking and harrowing even if you know it’s coming.


	The film is at its most vigorous here, when its possibilities lie ahead. In the few moments we see Vicentina before she’s told of this tragedy, the aged character hobbles around on her crutch and performs unassuming household tasks with a captivating, disaffected demeanor, as she curtly cuts off an incoming phone call (the dramatic irony of which only the viewer is aware). Something’s clearly on her mind, and we never need to know exactly what in order for her to feel familiar.

	Once she’s told of the tragedy by her younger neighbor Joana (Maíra Azevedo), the routine of having to answer questions and identify her son’s remains allows Faria to shift quickly into thorny territory, promising a film that lives within the rankling discomfort of loss. Wesley’s twin brother (also played by Novaes) briefly comes to visit, practically conjuring Wesley’s ghost as he wanders around the house. However, gossipy TV news stories speculate on Wesley’s intent and state of mind, foisting doubt upon the mourning matriarch as an intimate mystery fades into view. Her way of dealing with the ensuing guilt is to track down the families of the other victims and apologize on her son’s behalf, which, on paper, makes for a fascinating approach to grief, but proves rote and repetitive in execution.
	

	Across nearly two-and-a-half hours, the camera follows Vicentina — from an observant distance when she makes arduous journeys between neighborhoods, and then in closeup when she arrives — as she meets with family members one by one. Few of these sit-downs play out with meaningful differences until late into the runtime, during which Faria is shouldered with dramatic heavy lifting that doesn’t quite gel with her approach. She’s clearly adept at summoning despair when required, but behind the character’s rehearsed apology (which we hear spoken ad nauseam) is a near-identical approach to emoting that proves troublesome when repeated back to back. It’s a performance of loud thoughts writ large across her face, reeled in by pursed lips, resulting in the awkward effect of stilted emotions struggling to be expressed, when the film ought to be at its most volatile.

	A handful of those she visits offer riveting work in return — like Fábio Leal as a grieving, battered lover who harbors complicated feelings about his fiancé’s death — but Vicentina becomes a mere interloper to these lives, and they seldom affect her own sense of self, or her sense of contrition, in the process. Those who reject or question her motives are pushed far into the movie’s gradual, calculated unspooling, gesturing at thorny complexities which are never allowed to arise.

	The recurring appearance of a mysterious friend of Wesley’s, a death-metal frontman with dwarfism named Fred (a heartbreaking Giovanni Venturini), becomes vital to Vicentina understanding that he lived a life of unexpected interests and frustrations. But before these doubts and mysteries can be folded into her worldview, the focus pivots elsewhere, never allowing even dead ends and unanswered questions to emotionally linger, before the film wraps around to questions of how Vicentina is to live and cope going forward.

	Martins has a deft eye for place and environment. Many of the victims are poor, and his camera’s tour of Black Brazilian lives hints at a multifaceted cultural portrait not usually contained within the Brazilian cinema that takes hold in North America. (At least, not since “City of God.”) However, the fluidity of his exploration is hardened early on, thanks to a tedious focus on hitting the same beats with little variety or escalation. It is, at best, intriguing from a safe distance, where its detailed, rundown textures can tell you more about its characters’ struggles than up-close depiction of their inner lives ever does.

title: ‘One Battle After Another,’ ‘Frankenstein’ and ‘Avatar: Fire And Ash’ Among the Winners at MacGuffin Awards
description: The Property Masters Guild (PMG) honored “One Battle After Another,” “Frankenstein,” “Avatar: Fire and Ash” and more on Saturday for their standout
body:
The Property Masters Guild (PMG) honored “One Battle After Another,” “Frankenstein,” “Avatar: Fire and Ash” and more on Saturday for their standout props at the third annual MacGuffin Awards. 

	The Property Masters Guild works to raise awareness of the property master craft and the importance of design on productions. 

	“Property masters create character, build the worlds in which our stories play out and oftentimes our props drive the narrative itself,” co-chairs Corvino Elliott and Lauren Shell said. “Congratulations to all of our nominees and winners for standing out among your peers. The work you have done serves to remind the industry of just how much our voice matters.”
	

	Matthew Cavaliero and Robbie Duncan took home the award for Contemporary Feature Film for “One Battle After Another.” Christopher Geggie and his work on “Frankstein” won in the Period Feature Film category. The Fantasy Science Fiction Feature Film winners were Brad Elliott and Melissa Spicer for “Avatar: Fire and Ash.” 


	In television, “The ‘Burbs,” “Widow’s Bay,” “Spider-Noir,” “Fallout,” “Chief of War,” “Vampirina: Teenage Vampire” and “The Muppet Show” were honored. Sarah Snyder won the One-Hour Contemporary Television Series award for “The ’Burbs.” Nicole Ruby won the One-Hour Period Television Series award for “Spider-Noir.” Brad Einhorn and Andy Siegel earned the One-Hour Fantasy/Science Fiction Television Series award for “Fallout.” Morgan Kling won the Half-Hour Single-Camera Television Series award for “Widow’s Bay.” 
	

	The Humanitarian Award was presented to Luis Castro for his work as a food stylist. 

	Trish Reilly received the President’s Award for her contributions to the property craft and food styling on productions such as “Obi-Wan,” “Rebel Moon,” “The Orville,” “Grotesquerie” and “American Horror Story.”

	The Lifetime Achievement Award was presented to Barry Wilkinson for his career spanning more than four decades in the property department.

title: New York Knicks Player Jalen Brunson — Emmys Host Mariska Hargitay’s Buddy — Expected to Open Show (EXCLUSIVE)
description: As Monday’s 78th Emmys ceremony fast approaches, Variety has learned of two new highlights that viewers should expect to see: New York Knicks point
body:
As Monday’s 78th Emmys ceremony fast approaches, Variety has learned of two new highlights that viewers should expect to see: New York Knicks point guard Jalen Brunson is expected to appear via a pre-tape at the start of the telecast, while Reba McEntire has been tapped to perform a Dolly Parton song in tribute to the late icon.

	They join previously announced special segments including a “Charlie’s Angels” 50th anniversary reunion with stars Jaclyn Smith, Cheryl Ladd and Kate Jackson, as well as a “Buffy, the Vampire Slayer” 30th anniversary tribute with stars Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreanaz. Also lined up: Noah Kahan performing “Bridge Over Troubled Water” to accompany this year’s In Memoriam segment, while Julianna Margulies is expected to present the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award to Michael J. Fox.
	

	With New York Knicks superfan Mariska Hargitay as host, there’s been plenty of speculation about how the team might make an appearance during the Emmys — especially regarding pal Brunson. Hargitay herself has hinted in interviews that she hoped the Knicks would have a presence on the Emmys. She also recently told Variety at the HBO Max Emmy Nominee Celebration that Brunson would “definitely” be getting a role in “Law and Order: Special Victims Unit.”


	“It’s definitely happening,” Hargitay said of an “SVU” guest spot. “He’s kind of magnificent that way. He is just open and ready. I don’t think there is much Jalen can’t do.”

	When asked at last Thursday’s Emmys media day about whether Brunson would show up, executive producers Jesse Collins, Dionne Harmon and Jeannae Rouzan-Clay were coy: “She’s got a lot of friends,” Collins said. “Her contacts are deep.”
	

	From what Variety has heard, Brunson will appear at the very start of the show as part of a pre-taped number. Hargitay will then continue that performance live on stage, with dancers and other performers. That will then lead to Hargitay’s opening host monologue.

	Later in the evening, McEntire’s Parton tribute performance is expected to be introduced by Sally Field, who starred with Parton in 1989’s “Steel Magnolias.” Field will also be on hand as an Emmy nominee on Monday night, in the lead actress in a limited/anthology series or movie category for Netflix’s “Remarkably Bright Creatures.”

	McEntire and Parton, of course, were close friends for decades; among their music collabs was 2021’s “Does He Love You,” a reworking of a McEntire hit. McEntire is star of NBC’s “Happy’s Place.”

	Other presenters previously announced include “DTF St. Louis” stars Linda Cardellini and David Harbour, who won Emmys last weekend for outstanding limited/anthology actress and actor. Additionally lined up are Odessa A’zion, Macaulay Culkin, Alan Cumming, Sally Field, Jon Hamm, Marcello Hernández, Peter Krause, Dan Levy, Julianna Margulies, Annie Murphy, Niecy Nash-Betts, Keke Palmer, Amanda Peet, Amy Poehler, Florence Pugh, Rachel Sennott and Zendaya.

	And then announced on Sunday as presenters were Jamie Lee Curtis, Stephen Amell, Awkwafina, Noah Beck, Jessica Belkin, Scott Caan, Emma D’Arcy, Julia Garner, LL Cool J, Shailene Woodley, Hassie Harrison, Paul Anthony Kelly, Thaddeus LaGrone, John Mulaney, Brooks Nader, Emmy Rossum and Sofía Vergara. 

	Plus, expect Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson — stars of the upcoming Apple TV series “Brothers” — to appear together and one might assume, further milk the speculation that they might actually be related.

title: ‘Diary of a Mad Old Man’ Review: Wayne Wang and Fan Bingbing Unintentionally Find the Boredom in Sex and Death
description: Given its premise — a post-stroke retiree derives sexual pleasure from his daughter-in-law — the perverse qualities of Jun’ichirō Tanizaki’s classic
body:
Given its premise — a post-stroke retiree derives sexual pleasure from his daughter-in-law — the perverse qualities of Jun’ichirō Tanizaki’s classic “Diary of a Mad Old Man” are plentiful. But by the standards of contemporary mores, the 1961 novel isn’t particularly explicit; in his first feature since 2019, Wayne Wang initially takes a different approach, showing retired Utsugi (Lily Franky) furiously masturbating under his desk before ruefully giving up in the first shot. Consciously redirecting Tanizaki for new aims, the film makes thoughtful textual tweaks throughout, but the final product is counterintuitively dull.
	

	First-time screenwriter Kelvin Wyles follows the broad contours of Tanizaki’s text in the opening stretches while rewriting the novel’s first-person narration, deliberately softening the titular character’s selfish lucidity. The starting premise remains untouched: Utsugi is an intellectual retiree who, following a stroke, is solely motivated by lust for his daughter-in-law Satsuko (Fan Bingbing). With no expectation of sex, Utsugi instead avidly pursues toe-sucking access and voyeuristic glimpses of Satsuko in the shower, and spends a large amount on jewelry for her while withholding money from his children.


	Because the film introduces Utsugi in classical Japanese dress and takes eight minutes to show any characters wearing modern clothing, it’s not immediately clear that we’re watching a present-day rendition. But soon the updates come fast, from small details — Utsugi bonds with Satsuko while passing her vape back and forth — to greater sentimentalization of the characters. Tanizaki’s novel gains force from its first-person narrator’s unapologetically conveyed self-knowledge: “[E]ven though I am sentimental and given to tears — as virtuous as that may sound — my true nature is perverse and cold-hearted in the extreme.” 
	

	While still uncomfortably horny, this film’s Utsugi is softened: A newly concocted story where he examines otherwise useless paper scraps brought to him by a crow he nursed back to health, describing them as “precious proof of love,” is both irreconcilable with and less interesting than the egoist of Tanizaki’s novel, who’s made pitiable only by age and his debilitated condition.

	Wang has a great eye for maximizing production value. While limited primarily to the sets of a house, its outlying garden and an upscale bar cut off from all daylight, these nearly-all-interior worlds feel fully realized. (Exteriors and window shots place the film in Tokyo’s high-end Ginza district.) At age 62, Franky is meaningfully younger than his character but convincingly left-side-paralyzed throughout a performance that doesn’t lean into overstraining physical caricature. For her part, Satsuko is transformed from the novel’s fashionably dressed and gleefully exploitative figure to a more rounded character, complete with traumatic backstory conveyed via pensive monologue. This does not make her more interesting.

	As the film introduces all-new narratives, a possibility the novel never explicitly addressed is implicitly foregrounded, especially in a late confrontation with Utsugi’s son: The old man isn’t an end-of-life patient with nothing to lose finally fully acting on his desires, but instead suffering from late-stage dementia. That makes Wang’s film less a study of late-in-life misplaced desire from a lifelong morbid personality and more a work in conversation with depictions of elder-adult dementia and related sexual urges in recent films like Yoshida Daihachi’s “Teki Cometh,” Sarah Friedland’s “Familiar Touch” and Lance Hammer’s “Queen at Sea.” With graying populations and elder care an increasingly prevalent concern worldwide, “Diary of a Mad Old Man” is assuredly on schedule in finding this new use for the novel’s title.

	While the updated details remain thoughtful throughout, what’s been added to the previously lean narrative is turgid rather than transformative. To obtain the services of Fan Bingbing should be counted as something of a coup, casting which allows for subtextual frissons in two Japanese-Chinese relationships. Whatever the allegorical political/national possibilities, Satsuko’s relationships with both father and son are exploitation of a character from an impoverished background. None of these new wrinkles enriches or develops the text in new directions, as Tanizaki’s cold-blooded black comedy of malignant characters is replaced by Ozu-lite contemplations of death and long-take crying.

title: Courteney Cox Remembers ‘Scream’ Co-Star Hayden Panettiere: ‘She’s a Really Wonderful Actor’
description:

	While reflecting on he
body:
Courteney Cox has opened up about the death of her “Scream” co-star Hayden Panettiere, who died in August at 36 years old.

	While reflecting on her time filming “Scream VI” with Panettiere, Cox told Entertainment Weekly, “She’s a really wonderful actor. The last time I worked with her we had a great time. She was really fun and happy and smart, and it’s really sad. It’s obviously horrible.”


	Cox and Panettiere first starred together in 2011’s “Scream 4,” which introduced Panettiere to the franchise. The pair later reunited for 2023’s “Scream 6.”
	

	Tributes for Panettiere have continued to pour out across Hollywood. Most recently, her “Heroes” co-stars threw a reunion to “celebrate” her life.

	Along with photos of the event, series star Jimmy Jean-Louis shared on X, “A ‘HEROES’ reunion to celebrate the life of HAYDEN was deeply emotional. There was sadness in our hearts, but also so much love, gratitude and warmth as we remembered the beautiful moments shared and the lasting impact of a life that touched so many. Au revoir Hayden.”

	Jack Coleman, who played Panettiere’s dad on “Heroes,” posted his own emotional tribute on Instagram.

	“I’m heartbroken. I couldn’t begin to put my thoughts into words until now, and they will be inadequate,” Coleman wrote. “I’ve loved Hayden since day one of the pilot of ‘Heroes,’ 20 years ago, when she introduced herself by shouting ‘daddy’ and throwing her arms around me. From that day on, she called me daddio. She was Haydini, because she was a magician.”
	

	Shortly after her death, Panettiere’s father told ABC, “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden. She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen.”

title: John Stamos Delivers Emotional Speech About Fatherhood at Creative Coalition Awards
description: John Stamos teared up as he talked about fatherhood during an emotional speech Thursday at The Creative Coalition’s 12th Annual TV Humanitarian Awar
body:
John Stamos teared up as he talked about fatherhood during an emotional speech Thursday at The Creative Coalition’s 12th Annual TV Humanitarian Awards.

	Stamos has been an advocate with the child abuse treatment and prevention organization Childhelp for almost 40 years, but the meaning of his advocacy changed for him when he became a father for the first time eight years ago when his wife Caitlin McHugh gave birth to their son Billy.
	

	“Becoming a father has changed the way that I see children,” the “Full House” star said, choking up. “You look at your own kid and you realize how much they depend on us to make them feel safe and loved and protected, and then you realize there are so many children that don’t have that. Once you really let that in, it’s hard to look away.”


	Stamos’s best friend, comedian Jeffrey Ross, presented him with the Creative Coalition award.

	“Every portion of my life, I’ve been given a career and a platform more attention than any grown man who played Uncle Jesse deserves,” Stamos said. “So if I can take a little of that attention and point it toward children who need us, this feels less like charity and more like responsibility.”



	

					Caitlin McHugh, John Stamos and son Billy celebrate Billy’s eighth birthday at Monster Jam at SoFi Stadium on April 11 in Inglewood, California.
									Getty Images for Feld Entertainm
	



	Earlier in the evening, on the red carpet, Stamos spoke about the upcoming release of “Love From Above,” a children’s book he wrote with Billy. The book, with watercolor paintings from Stamos, chronicles grappling with the loss of John’s parents and feeling their presence in the form of hummingbirds.
	

	“We have this folklore in our family, when my father passed away, there was a hummingbird in my dad’s garden, [Billy] said ‘There’s your dad,’” Stamos told Variety. “I’m like ‘That’s a hummingbird.’ He said, ‘No, that’s your dad coming back to make sure we’re taking care of his garden.’ And so it’s been stuck in our family.”

	The book will be released April 20, 2027.

	“Billy’s been very busy, taking it very seriously, it’s the cutest thing I’ve ever seen,” Stamos said. “We’re excited to go out and read it to kids, we’re excited to go to hospitals where we can, schools. Hopefully it’ll help kids who have maybe lost their grandparents.”



	

					Patrick Ball and Simran Baidwan attend The Creative Coalition’s 12th Annual Humanitarian Awards Dinner at VERSE LA on September 10.
									Getty Images for The Creative Co
	



	Also honored at the event, which was hosted by Variety’s Marc Malkin, were Simran Baidwan (executive producer and writer for “The Pitt”), Famke Janssen (“X-Men”), Cara Buono (“Stranger Things”), Lisa Ann Walter (“Abbott Elementary”) and Mary Lou Belli (director of “The Ms. Pat Show”).

	Baidwan’s award was presented to her by “The Pitt” fan-favorite Patrick Ball, also known as Dr. Langdon.

	“On ‘The Pitt,’ she helped bring something particularly important out of the shadows: family caregiving,” Ball said. “Millions of people are caregivers. I know a few of them. Although many of them would never call themselves that. They’re just the ones who show up … Simran understood that these lives, these quiet daily acts of devotion and exhaustion and sacrifice and grace, these lives deserve to be seen and they deserve to be celebrated.”



	

					Lisa Ann Walter and Sheryl Lee Ralph attend The Creative Coalition’s 12th Annual Humanitarian Awards Dinner at VERSE LA on Sept. 10, 2026, in Los Angeles.
									Jesse Grant
	



	Baidwan said, “The tireless work and sacrifices of caregivers affect everyday Americans everywhere and by highlighting their journeys to a story, perhaps we can help restore a little hope in humanity along the way.”

	Like Baidwan, Walter has been recognizing and participating in small but important acts of service for as long as she can remember. Her co-star and close friend Sheryl Lee Ralph presented the award, sharing how Walter was marching against the Vietnam War at age six and fighting for women’s equality at age eight and has shown up ever since.
	

	“I don’t advocate for reproductive rights because I’m the owner of a reproductive system,” Walter said. “I was an advocate for gender equity because anything else, even as a child, seemed to me to be stupid and unfair.”



	

					Scott Bakula and Mary Lou Belli attend The Creative Coalition’s 12th Annual Humanitarian Awards Dinner.
									Getty Images for The Creative Co
	



	Belli, who received the award from Scott Bakula, expressed her gratitude for her decades of service and mentorship to young filmmakers being noticed.

	“When I found out I was getting this award, I literally wept,” Belli said. “And two weeks before that, I found out I would have been nominated for my fourth Emmy and I had none of that reaction to that.”

	See more photos from the TV Humanitarian Awards below.



	

					Fiona Dourif and Katherine LaNasa attend The Creative Coalition’s 12th Annual Humanitarian Awards Dinner at VERSE LA.
									Getty Images for The Creative Co

body:
Steve McBee Sr.
                          Home After Prison Release ...
                          Reunites With Family
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 13, 2026
                            7:24 AM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Steve McBee Sr. is back home and back with his family after spending months behind bars ... and the 'McBee Dynasty' patriarch is making it clear he’s appreciating the little things.
      
    
            Steve shared his first public message following his release Saturday, posting a video from his return to the family farm in Gallatin, Missouri. The reality star expressed gratitude for being home and for the blessings in his life.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            His return has been an emotional one for the McBee family. Steve’s son, Steven McBee Jr., celebrated his dad’s release online, while another son, Cole McBee, shared a photo of Steve meeting his newest granddaughter, Tate, who was born while he was incarcerated.
      

            Steve’s freedom comes after he served less than a year of a two-year federal prison sentence. He began his sentence in December 2025 at a federal prison camp in South Dakota after pleading guilty to a federal crop insurance fraud scheme.
      
    
            According to court records, Steve admitted to a scheme involving millions of dollars in crop insurance benefits. He was ultimately ordered to pay more than $4 million in restitution and forfeit more than $3 million to the government.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Steve could have faced a much longer sentence, but the judge ultimately sentenced him to 24 months behind bars, followed by two years of supervised release.
      
    
            His early release was made possible in part by his participation in a program that reduced the amount of time he had to spend in prison. He is expected to spend several months under home confinement.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Steve's legal troubles have been a major storyline on Bravo's "The McBee Dynasty: Real American Cowboys," with cameras documenting the impact his incarceration had on his family and their Missouri farming operation.
      
    
            Before reporting to prison, Steve characterized the experience as something of a “sabbatical” and maintained that he accepted responsibility for his actions.
      
    
            As we previously reported, according to court docs obtained by TMZ, a federal judge denied Steve’s effort to get the civil suit brought by the U.S. government against him tossed out of court -- Steve claimed the government had no case.
      
    
            Now, after months apart, Steve is finally getting what his family has been waiting for ... a chance to be home together again.
